p: Wednesday, January 5, Maria opened a blank document and typed: Cascade Valley Health, Information Technology Strategic Plan, 2028 to 2030. Then she stopped.

The last one was in the shared drive. Ochoa had written it three years ago, 2025 to 2027, forty pages with his name on the cover. She read it at her desk with a cup of coffee going cold. Every initiative had a date beside it, and nearly every date had a check mark. MedaLink was on page thirty-one, in one line: assess options before end of support. Somebody had done that. It had taken her fifteen months.
She'd never written a CIO's plan. She'd never been in the room when one was written. And the board would read this one as Ochoa's, whoever typed it.

That afternoon she went down the hall to ask him where to start. His door was open and his chair was empty. The bookshelf behind his desk had gaps in it. Marcus had come up from the basement that morning carrying an interface engine manual from 1998. Ochoa had given it to him, and Marcus said it was wrong about everything and he was keeping it anyway.
Her phone buzzed on the walk back. Lucia. med surg starts monday. hospital, real patients. what do i bring
Maria typed the first true thing she thought of. Two pens that work. A watch with a second hand. Eat before you go. A minute later: that's it? That's most of it.

Back at her desk she wrote one question under the title, the one Ochoa had asked her in April about the business case. Who reads this in 2030? Then she sat looking at it for a long time, because she didn't know.

Monday, January 10, Maria had nine pages and no plan yet. Kiran had sent her a spreadsheet of every open request from every hospital, forty-four rows. Corvane had sent its product roadmap for the next three years, with a cover note from Brett. Aisha had sent a list titled What We Should Be Doing, and it was good.

Ochoa's old plan sat open in the other window. Three sources, and all of them were somebody's list. She could see a plan that was mostly a long table of projects with prices beside them. It would be done by Friday.

She pulls Cascade's strategic plan, five goals, and writes each across the top of a page. Then a current state assessment, one page per area: applications, infrastructure, people, spending, risks. Rawlins is in it twice, once for the network and once for the locks. Only then does she open Kiran's spreadsheet, and each of his forty-four rows gets the goal it serves, or a blank. Eleven rows stay blank. Kiran reads them and laughs a little. Four of those are mine.

Thursday, January 13, the chief executive of Snowy Range Community Health called from Laramie. Her health center wasn't part of Cascade. It ran six clinics in two counties, saw anyone who walked in, and charged on a sliding scale by income. About a third of its patients had no insurance. Its old EHR vendor had just been bought, and the price had doubled.
Half our patients end up at your hospitals, she said. We'd like to come onto your Corvane. Corvane says big customers can host small ones. Could you put us in your plan?
Kiran was already thinking about the build. We have forty clinics on Corvane. It'd be forty-six. Same build.

Maria puts it in the plan's second year as a hosted partner, with its own line. A hosting agreement and a business associate agreement, written with Joan. Its own records and access, walled off from Cascade's except where a patient's care crosses over. Sliding fee billing and its federal grant reports in the build. A seat at the clinical informatics council. The chief executive reads the draft and says it's the first time a hospital system asked what her patients needed instead of what her clinics cost.

Tuesday, January 18, the three Wyoming CNOs and the system's chief nursing officer read the people section of Maria's draft. Gail had circled one line in pencil. Nursing informatics: covered by the vice president of clinical systems.

That's you, Gail said. You've been our nursing informatics officer for fifteen months, and it isn't anybody's job. Aisha has a title for the doctors. We don't. She let that sit. Denise Harmon asked me last week whether anybody was ever going to write that job.

She writes it into the plan's first year. A chief nursing information officer, reporting to the system CNO with a dotted line to the CIO. Co-chair of the council with Aisha. Owns nursing documentation, BCMA practice, and nurse adoption. She wrote it knowing it was the part of the job she'd miss, which was how she knew it had to be somebody's whole job. IT builds what that role and the council decide. Gail reads it and taps the dotted line. That's the part that makes it real.
Thursday, January 20, Glenn's year-end report came in at 7:02, the way his emails always did.

An email from Glenn Morrow. Subject: Clinical systems, 2027. Maria, your 2027 operating budget was $18.4 million. Actual was $19.55 million. The board's finance committee will see this line in March, the same month it sees your plan. I'd like to understand it before they do. Glenn
He'd added a line under his name. Your business case held. Let's see if your budget did.

Kiran had the drivers by noon. Go-live overtime and superuser backfill, $820,000. The ransomware response and the insurance deductible, $250,000. The second Rawlins circuit, started early, $180,000 for the year. Cascade's MedaLink support contract, no longer needed after cutover, ended a month early, which saved $100,000.

One page. The total, 6.25 percent over. Then each driver, marked one-time or recurring. The go-live, the ransomware, and MedaLink's early end were one-time, $970,000 net. The circuit recurs, $180,000 a year that the 2028 budget never had. She adds it to the 2028 reforecast with a line about why. Glenn reads it at his desk. So what recurs is a hundred and eighty thousand. And it's in next year's budget now.

Tuesday, January 25, the forty-four requests came to the IT steering committee. Together they needed about 61,000 analyst hours over three years. After support and upgrades, Maria's team had about 38,000.

Each hospital president had sent one email about their own request. The Fort Collins president had sent two. Aisha's predictive program was on the list, and so was Nate's security work from Rawlins, and so was Snowy Range.

Mandatory work goes first: Nate's security list and two regulatory changes. The rest get scored against the five goals, risk, and value, then stacked against the 38,000 hours. Twenty-six land above the line. Eighteen land below it, each with a date to come back or a plain no and the reason. Maria sends every hospital president the whole list, not just their own row. The Fort Collins president calls, annoyed. Then he asks what would move his request up, and she tells him.

Thursday, February 3, two days after Maria sent Ochoa her draft, Glenn's analyst brought a benchmark. A national survey of health systems put IT operating spending at a median of 3.1 percent of revenue. Cascade spent $46.8 million on $1.8 billion, 2.6 percent.
Aisha saw it before lunch. Put it on page one, she wrote. We're nine million under our peers. That pays for my whole program.
Tasha had sent one too. The service desk fixed 70 percent of calls on the first contact. The survey's median was 78.

Glenn's analyst rebuilds the peer group: multi-hospital systems with rural sites and no medical school, on the same definition of IT spending. The median drops to 2.8. Cascade is 0.2 points under, not 0.5. Tasha checks the desk number the same way. The survey counts password resets the phone system fixes on its own, and Cascade doesn't. Matched, the desk median is 74, so Cascade's 70 is a real gap, just a smaller one. The plan shows both gaps with their definitions, beside the outcomes. Aisha sighs. Three point six million is still three point six million. And Glenn will believe it.

Tuesday, February 8, Aisha brought the Sepsis Predict results to Maria's office. Corvane's model had run silently since the April upgrade at the eight Corvane hospitals, and since October in Wyoming, scoring every patient and showing no one.

Corvane's brochure said its area under the curve was 0.87. Kiran had checked it against the residents' chart reviews, hospital by hospital. Greeley, 0.85. Fort Collins, 0.83. Cheyenne, 0.79. Rawlins, 0.68, on nineteen septic patients since October.
Overall it's 0.81, Aisha said. I want it live in all eleven on April first. It's the first thing in my section of the plan.

Greeley and Fort Collins go live in April, with a threshold Kiran and Aisha pick from Cascade's own two by two. Cheyenne stays silent until it has more cases. Rawlins stays silent, and Aisha reads the nineteen charts to find out why. Every quarter, a named owner checks it by site. Aisha takes the plan line back and rewrites it herself. Two sites, then earn the rest.

Monday, February 14, Joan called at 8:40. A first-year resident had asked her, politely, whether it was all right to paste patient notes into a free AI chatbot on his phone to draft discharge summaries. He'd been doing it for a month. So had three other residents.
He asked, Joan said. That's the good news. We have no policy that says no, and nothing in your plan that says what yes looks like.
Nate was on the line too. Penwright's AI is approved, with a business associate agreement, he said. This one isn't. They can't tell the difference from the screen.

Before noon, Aisha tells the four residents to stop today, and why. Joan runs her assessment on their month. Maria drafts the policy with Joan, Nate, Aisha, and legal. Approved AI tools only, each with a BAA. No patient information in public ones. New AI tools come through the technology intake. Training for every clinician, an owner, and a review in a year. It goes to the policy committee in March, and into the plan as its own line. The resident who asked helps write the training.

Thursday, February 17, Maria wrote Kiran's job down. The plan needed it. Every year of the roadmap leaned on the same two things: clinical content that stayed current, and superusers who could teach. Kiran had been doing both since October, on top of everything else, and nobody had written any of it down.

Halfway down the page she stopped at the line for skills. Year two brought Meadowlark's patch data and other outside tools into the chart through FHIR. Years two and three took Sepsis Predict to the other hospitals, and after Monday's call about the residents and the chatbot, somebody had to be able to judge every AI tool that came in. The last class anyone on her team had taken was Corvane's build training for One Chart. Most of what they knew about FHIR, they'd learned from Marcus at a whiteboard.

She asked Kiran to her office at four, so he'd have to leave at five. He came in with a notebook, as if it were a meeting about somebody else. When she showed him the skills line, he nodded. I've been reading about the sepsis model at night, he said. I can keep up.

They build it together before five. Maria lists what the plan needs by year: FHIR apps, model validation, AI tool review, and the content work. Kiran rates himself and the team against it, honestly, on his third try. Each person gets a development plan with four protected hours a week on the schedule, a paid certification where the role needs one, and a review every January. Not at night, Maria says. Tuesday afternoons, on the schedule, where I can see it. Then the role page itself. Clinical content and superuser program lead. He runs the council's content process and the train the trainer program. He doesn't own clinical content, the clinicians do. He isn't on call; the team rotates. Yesenia, the analyst Marcus taught first, is his deputy, and she shadows him on content until she can cover it. The skills the role keeps current are on the page, with the hours to learn them. Kiran reads to the bottom. You wrote my hours into a job description. Somebody had to.

Tuesday, February 22, Marcus came up from the basement at seven with a binder under his arm. Four inches thick, tabbed in three colors, RELAY on the spine in his block capitals. He set it on Maria's desk.
He sat down without being asked, which he did now. Good binder, he said. It was what he'd said about the one in Omaha.

Then he told her. His granddaughter in Tucson had a brother now. He wanted four days a week starting in July, and to be done for good at the end of 2030. Your plan says Relay runs through 2030, he said. Somebody has to run it after. I want it in writing who. And I want it in writing that I'm here till I say I'm not.

They write it together that morning. Two named successors: the other analyst he's been teaching, and a second he picks himself. Every Relay skill in his binder gets a sign-off date for each of them, the hardest last. From July he's principal interface engineer, four days a week, teaching, through December 2030, and the last line says the date moves only if he moves it. Maria signs it. Marcus reads the last line again. This in my file? It's in the plan.
Tuesday, March 7, at 7:30, Ochoa didn't have a legal pad. He had her plan, eighty pages, with his initials on every one.
I'm retiring, he said. March thirty-first. I told the board chair in July. On Friday I'm going to tell the rest of them, and I'm going to recommend you as interim CIO. They'll decide. Not me.

Maria didn't say anything for a while. She thought about the go or no-go meeting, and the command center in Cheyenne, and the exit conference at Greeley a year and a half ago. Every time, he'd taken a chair along the wall. You sat along the wall all year, she said.
I told you I'd be furniture, he said. I didn't say it was practice. Then, plainer: If I'd told you in October, you'd have run go-live for me. You ran it for Rawlins. I needed to know you would.

Irene told me in January, Maria said. I didn't hear it. That's what Irene's for. She looked at his initials, one on every page. Who do I call at two in the morning? Nobody. You built it so nobody has to.

Wednesday she drove to Greeley to see Bev's pilot before Friday. The remote station sat at the charge desk on the fourth floor, where the fax machine used to be: two screens, two Rawlins beds, a headset. Bev was in the chair. Kid. You look like you're about to take report. Ochoa's retiring. Bev slid the headset down around her neck and looked at her a long moment. Then take it.

Gail wanted Bev's numbers in Friday's plan. Five weeks, twenty-six patients watched. Five went to Greeley. In the same five weeks last year, twelve of twenty-nine similar patients had made the three-hour ride. Transfers cut by more than half, Gail had written. Put that on the slide.

The slide says five of twenty-six this year, twelve of twenty-nine last year, five weeks in, too early to call. Beside it are the balancing measures. One patient kept at Rawlins had to transfer the next morning. Nights at both units are surveyed too. The six-month review date sits at the bottom. Bev reads it over Maria's shoulder. That's how I'd chart it. Gail, on the phone, says fine, and that she'll say promising.

Friday, March 10, the board met at two on the sixth floor. Ochoa spoke first, for four minutes. He was retiring at the end of the month. He recommended Maria Santos as interim CIO, and the board would take it up in executive session after the plan. Then he went and sat along the wall.
Maria led with the ask: approve the plan, and $3 million in new capital for its first year. Twenty minutes in, she reached the capital page, and the room split.

Patients die of sepsis, not firewalls, Aisha said. She wanted $2.2 million: Sepsis Predict, Bev's remote ICU at Laramie, and Meadowlark for four hundred patients. A clinic in Rawlins was closed for a week, Glenn said. He wanted $2.4 million for Nate's security list first. Together that was $4.6 million. Every face at the table turned to Maria.

You're both talking about the same thing, she says. The night nobody's watching. Then she asks them for the criteria, not the money: harm prevented, how sure we are, and when we'd know. Both write theirs on the same page. Measured that way, the plan is $1.6 million for the security items Nate rates high, now. $200,000 to take Sepsis Predict live at Greeley and Fort Collins. $1.2 million for the remote ICU and Meadowlark, released in September if the pilots meet the measures they set in advance. Glenn checks the sum. Aisha checks the gate. The board votes yes.
The board went into executive session at 3:40. Maria waited in the hallway outside with Aisha and Glenn, the three of them standing by the window with nothing to do, which none of them was good at.

September, Aisha said finally. If Bev's numbers hold, I get my money. If they hold, Glenn said. I wrote the gate. I'll be the first one to open it. Aisha looked at him like she was deciding whether that was a joke. It wasn't, and she seemed to like that better.

At 4:15 the board chair came out. The board had named Maria Santos interim chief information officer, starting Monday, April 3. Interim, he said. For a year. After what happened at Rawlins, the audit committee will want to see what you do with security and privacy. Then we'll talk about the rest. He shook her hand. Ray says you'll tell us the truth early. Do that.
Ochoa walked her to her car, the way he had in Greeley the day the survey ended. Sundays, he said. Seven thirty. Bring the legal pad. I'll still make you write. Who pays? The one with the job.
She called Irene from the car. Interim, she said. For a year. Did you write it for the night shift?
I tried. Then they'll tell you.

The next week the board secretary sent the conflict of interest form every officer signs. Under gifts from vendors in the last two years, Maria wrote none, and attached Pam's log, which said declined and disclosed, April 2027. It was the easiest page in the stack.
Friday, March 31, Ochoa's last day, there was no party. He'd said no to one. At five he walked out the front door with one box, like anybody else.
Monday morning, Maria Santos had been the interim CIO for forty minutes when the letter arrived.

The office was at the far end of the fourth floor hall. The nameplate still said the last person's name. On the windowsill was a small jade plant that hadn't been there before, with an index card in front of it in Ochoa's handwriting. Water it every other Sunday. R.O.
The letter had come in an envelope, handwritten, addressed to the CIO, and the mailroom had sent it up.

Letter from a Rawlins night nurse. Dear Ms. Santos,. I've been a night nurse on the medical floor in Rawlins for nineteen years. Somebody told me you worked nights in Greeley, so you'll know what I mean. For most of those years, at three in the morning, I was the only one awake who could check anything. Last Tuesday a man on my floor went bad at ten after three. A nurse in Greeley saw his pressure drop on her screen and called me before the monitor alarmed. A pharmacist in Cheyenne checked his antibiotic before I hung it. When we sent him to Greeley, I didn't fax anything. They opened his chart, and it was all there, every page. I don't know how much of that was you. My charge nurse says some of it. I wanted somebody to know I'm not the only one awake anymore.. Connie, RN, nights

Maria read it twice. Then she took a picture of it and sent it to Ochoa, with one line: I assume you've seen this. He replied in under a minute. I haven't. It's why you have that office. Sunday, 7:30. Bring it.
Her phone buzzed again. Lucia, who was supposed to be in pharmacology. how's the bigger office. do u have a plant yet
Ochoa left me one, she typed. I have instructions.
The next one took longer. fall rotations posted. ICU. greeley. 4th floor.
Maria read the last line of the letter again. I'm not the only one awake anymore. Then she took a fresh legal pad out of the desk drawer, wrote 2030 at the top, and picked up her phone.
